pages.x: Jan Hus, a priest in Prague, preached in Czech, not Latin, and attacked the wealth and corruption of the church. Summoned to a church council at Constance with a promise of safe conduct, he was arrested, tried for heresy, and burned at the stake in 1415. In Bohemia he became a martyr.

On 30 July 1419 a crowd of Hussites marched on Prague's New Town Hall to free prisoners, and threw the councillors out of the windows, killing several of them: the first defenestration of Prague. The king died weeks later, and Bohemia rose in revolt.

The Hussites' general, Jan Žižka, had lost one eye in his youth, and lost the other in battle. He turned farm wagons into moving forts, chained together and packed with crossbowmen and men with early handguns, and he never lost a battle. His peasant armies beat the knights of Europe.

The emperor Sigismund and the pope sent five crusades against the Hussites between 1420 and 1431, and every one failed. At Domažlice in 1431, it is said, the crusaders ran as soon as they heard the Hussites singing their battle hymn as they came: You who are the warriors of God.
The Hussites called their handguns píšťala, a Czech word for a pipe or whistle. The word travelled into German and other languages, and is probably where the word pistol comes from.

In the end the Hussites split. Moderates made peace with the church, which allowed them to take communion with the cup as well as the bread. In 1434 they joined Catholic lords to crush the radicals at Lipany, and two years later Sigismund was accepted as king.

The Hussites broke with Rome a century before Luther, and their church lasted two hundred years. Luther later said: we are all Hussites without knowing it. A statue of Hus stands in Prague's Old Town Square, and 6 July, the day he died, is a national holiday.
